notes.front: In the Prometheus documentation, what is a metric?
notes.back: A numerical measurement, in layperson’s terms — such as request times, active connections or query counts.
notes.explanation: Metrics turn behaviour into numbers you can track over time, which is what lets Prometheus alert on them and graph them.
notes.example: Like a car’s dashboard gauges: speed, fuel and temperature are all metrics, each a single number that changes over time.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus time series?
notes.back: A stream of timestamped values that all belong to the same metric name and the same set of labels.
notes.explanation: Prometheus stores everything as time series, so two samples with a different label set count as different series, even under the same metric name.
notes.example: Like a spreadsheet column that only ever holds one server’s request count, timestamped row by row.

notes.front: In OpenTelemetry’s observability primer, what is a log?
notes.back: A timestamped message emitted by services or other components, not necessarily tied to any one request.
notes.explanation: That last part is what separates logs from traces: a log can appear with no request or transaction attached to it at all.
notes.example: Like entries in a lighthouse keeper’s logbook: each one is dated, but most aren’t about any one passing ship.

notes.front: In OpenTelemetry, what is a span?
notes.back: A single unit of work or operation, tracking what happened during the time it was executed.
notes.explanation: Spans are the building blocks traces are made of, each one covering one step of a request.
notes.example: Like one leg of a relay race: it has its own start, its own runner and its own finish, even though it’s part of a longer race.

notes.front: What is a distributed trace?
notes.back: The record of the path a single request takes as it propagates through multiple services, made up of one or more spans.
notes.explanation: Traces exist because no single log line shows a request’s whole journey; the trace stitches the spans back together.
notes.example: Like a parcel’s tracking history across depots: one combined trail, even though a different depot handled each leg.

notes.front: What is a span event?
notes.back: A structured log message or annotation on a span, marking a meaningful, singular point in time during that span’s duration.
notes.explanation: A span covers a duration; a span event is a marker inside it, used when the exact moment matters more than the interval.
notes.example: Like a mile marker on a road trip: the trip (span) has a start and end, but the marker records one precise point along it.

notes.front: What are span attributes?
notes.back: Key-value pairs of metadata attached to a span to describe the operation it tracks.
notes.explanation: For a span that tracks adding an item to a shopping cart, attributes might record the user’s ID, the item’s ID and the cart ID.
notes.example: Like luggage tags on a suitcase: each tag (attribute) adds a fact about the item without changing the suitcase itself.

notes.front: What is a span context?
notes.back: An immutable object on every span holding its trace ID, its own span ID, trace flags and trace state.
notes.explanation: It’s the part of a span that is serialized and carried along as the request moves between services.
notes.example: Like a shipping label glued to a parcel: it travels with the parcel and identifies which shipment and leg it belongs to.

notes.front: What is context propagation, in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: The core mechanism that lets spans be correlated with each other and assembled into a trace, wherever they were generated.
notes.explanation: Without it, each service’s spans would be islands; propagation is what carries the trace ID across service boundaries.
notes.example: Like a baton passed hand to hand in a relay: whoever is holding it knows which race it belongs to.

notes.front: What is Prometheus’s pull model?
notes.back: Prometheus fetches (scrapes) metrics from targets over HTTP, rather than targets sending metrics to it.
notes.explanation: Pulling is how Prometheus normally collects data: the server decides when to scrape each target. The Overview lists “time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP” among its main features.
notes.example: Like a postal round where the courier visits each house to collect mail, rather than every house posting mail in separately.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Overview, “Features”; FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: What is the push model, as Prometheus’s FAQ contrasts it with pulling?
notes.back: Targets send their own metrics to the monitoring system, instead of the system fetching them.
notes.explanation: Prometheus mostly avoids this model; where pushing is unavoidable, it offers an intermediary, the Pushgateway.
notes.example: Like every house posting its own mail into the post office, rather than a courier doing the rounds.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: What does a static_config do in a Prometheus scrape configuration?
notes.back: It specifies a fixed list of targets and a common set of labels to attach to everything scraped from them.
notes.explanation: It’s the canonical way to name targets by hand, as opposed to discovering them dynamically.
notes.example: Like writing a fixed guest list for a party, instead of letting people arrive and be added on the door.

notes.front: What is file-based service discovery in Prometheus?
notes.back: A mechanism that reads target lists from files on disk, detecting changes via disk watches and applying them immediately.
notes.explanation: It’s a generic interface: any tool that can write target lists to files can feed Prometheus, which is how custom service discovery mechanisms plug in.
notes.example: Like a noticeboard a caretaker checks continuously and updates the guest list from — anyone can pin a new sheet to it.

notes.front: What does Kubernetes service discovery let Prometheus do?
notes.back: Retrieve scrape targets from the Kubernetes REST API and stay synchronised with the cluster’s state automatically.
notes.explanation: Unlike a static_config, it needs no manual updates: targets appear and disappear as the cluster itself changes.
notes.example: Like a guest list that updates itself in real time as people arrive at and leave a building.

notes.front: What is a service level indicator (SLI)?
notes.back: A measurement of a service’s behaviour, ideally taken from the perspective of the service’s own users.
notes.explanation: It’s the raw number a later target will be measured against, such as how fast a page loads for real users.
notes.example: Like a thermometer reading: on its own it’s just a measurement, not yet a target.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: What is a service level objective (SLO)?
notes.back: The way reliability is communicated to the organisation and other teams, by attaching one or more SLIs to business value.
notes.explanation: Where an SLI is just a measurement, an SLO turns it into a goal that others can be held to.
notes.example: Like agreeing the thermometer reading should stay under 38°C, not just recording what it reads.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: What is a service level agreement (SLA)?
notes.back: A contract with users, written or implied, that sets out what happens when the service meets or misses the SLOs inside it.
notes.explanation: A quick test: ask what follows if the SLOs are missed. If nothing explicit does, it is almost certainly an SLO, not an SLA.
notes.example: Like a gym membership that refunds a month’s fee if the pool is closed for more than a week: the pool’s opening promise is the SLO, and the refund is what makes it an SLA.
notes.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4, “Service Level Objectives”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Prometheus metrics are, in the documentation’s own words, {{c1::numerical measurements}}.
notes.explanation: This plain-language definition is what lets any number — request counts, active connections, temperatures — become a metric.

notes.front: A billing system needs to charge customers per request, with no gaps or duplicates. Should it rely on Prometheus metrics for this?
notes.back: No. Prometheus values reliability over 100% accuracy, so it is not a good choice for per-request billing.
notes.explanation: The collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough for exact accounting; a dedicated billing system suits it better.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Overview, “When does it not fit?”

notes.front: A Prometheus time series is uniquely identified by its {{c1::metric name and its set of labels}}.
notes.explanation: Change any label’s value, or add or remove one, and Prometheus starts a new time series rather than continuing the old one.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A time series is being scraped as http_requests_total{method="GET"}. A new status label is then added, so it becomes http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200"}. Is this still the same time series?
notes.back: No. Adding a label changes the label set, so Prometheus treats it as a new time series.
notes.explanation: The data model says changing any label’s value, including adding or removing labels, creates a new time series.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: Unlike traces, logs aren’t necessarily associated with any particular {{c1::user request or transaction}}.
notes.explanation: That’s what makes a bare log harder to use for debugging one specific request: nothing ties it to that request on its own.

notes.front: A support engineer has one log line, “Failed login attempt”, with no trace or span reference attached. Can they tell which user request produced it, from the log alone?
notes.back: Not reliably. Logs aren’t necessarily tied to any one request, and become far more useful once correlated with a trace and span.
notes.explanation: The primer says logs become far more useful when they are part of a span, or correlated with a trace and a span: that link, not the log text, supplies the missing context.

notes.front: A log line is JSON with the same field names and types on every message, such as timestamp, level and service. What kind of log is this?
notes.back: A structured log: it has a defined, consistent schema that downstream systems can reliably parse.
notes.explanation: Valid JSON alone isn’t enough to make a log structured — it’s the stable schema of field names and types that does.

notes.front: A log line reads: “[ERROR] 2024-08-04 12:45:23 - Failed to connect to database. Exception: java.sql.SQLException: Timeout expired.” What kind of log is this?
notes.back: An unstructured log: it has no consistent structure, so parsing it at scale takes extra work, such as regular expressions and custom parsers.
notes.explanation: Unstructured logs are often more human-readable, which is why they’re common in development, but they’re harder to analyse in production.

notes.front: A service logs key=value lines such as level=ERROR service=user-authentication userId=12345 message="Failed login attempt", and other services log different keys, with no shared schema. What kind of log is this?
notes.back: A semistructured log: it has machine-readable key/value pairs, but no guaranteed stable schema across every message.
notes.explanation: Semistructured logs are usually easier to parse than unstructured ones, but may still need mapping and type coercion before analysis.

notes.front: According to the Prometheus FAQ, how should you feed logs into Prometheus?
notes.back: Don’t. Prometheus is a system to collect and process metrics, not an event logging system.
notes.explanation: The FAQ’s own short answer is literally “Don’t!”, pointing instead to a dedicated logging system such as Grafana Loki.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “How to feed logs into Prometheus?”

notes.front: A team wants to store and search application log lines. Should they send those logs directly into Prometheus, or into a system like Grafana Loki?
notes.back: Into a system like Grafana Loki. Prometheus’s own FAQ says not to feed logs into it, since it processes metrics, not log events.
notes.explanation: Loki, or a similar log store, is built for the very thing Prometheus’s FAQ says it is not: storing and querying event logs.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “How to feed logs into Prometheus?”

notes.front: Besides a name and start and end timestamps, an OpenTelemetry span can carry {{c1::span events}}: structured log messages that mark single points in time during the span.
notes.explanation: A span also holds a span context, attributes, span links, a span status and, unless it is the root span, a parent span ID.

notes.front: A page load passes through an API gateway, a backend service and a database. What single unit of work does each of these three steps represent, on its own?
notes.back: A span. Each step is one span, and together the three spans form a single trace.
notes.explanation: A span tracks one operation from start to finish; stitching several spans together end to end is what makes a trace.

notes.front: A trace is made of one or more spans, and the first span in it, with no parent, is called the {{c1::root span}}.
notes.explanation: Every other span in the trace points back to a parent, directly or indirectly, until that chain reaches the root.

notes.front: Three services each produce their own span for one user request. What links those three separate spans into a single distributed trace?
notes.back: They share the same trace ID, carried between services by context propagation.
notes.explanation: Without that shared ID travelling with the request, the three spans would just be unconnected records in three different places.

notes.front: A span event is best used to mark a meaningful, {{c1::singular point in time}} during a span’s duration, rather than an interval.
notes.explanation: That’s the deciding factor: if the exact timestamp matters, use a span event; if it doesn’t, attach the data as a span attribute instead.

notes.front: A page becomes interactive partway through loading, and you want to record the exact moment this happens. Should you record it as a span attribute or a span event?
notes.back: A span event, because the timestamp of that moment is what’s meaningful here, not just the data.
notes.explanation: OpenTelemetry’s own guidance is to attach data as a span event when its timestamp is meaningful, and as an attribute when it isn’t.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Traces, “When to use span events versus span attributes”

notes.front: A service makes an outgoing HTTP call to another service and waits for the reply. What span kind does OpenTelemetry give that span?
notes.back: Client. A client span represents a synchronous outgoing remote call, such as an outgoing HTTP request or database call.
notes.explanation: “Synchronous” here doesn’t mean blocking code or async/await; it means the call is made now, not queued for later processing.

notes.front: A service receives an incoming HTTP request and handles it. What span kind does OpenTelemetry give that span?
notes.back: Server. A server span represents a synchronous incoming remote call, such as an incoming HTTP request or remote procedure call.
notes.explanation: The parent of a server span is usually a remote client span on the caller’s side of the same call.

notes.front: A function call inside a service does work without ever crossing a process boundary. What span kind does OpenTelemetry give that span?
notes.back: Internal. Internal spans represent operations that don’t cross a process boundary, such as an instrumented function call.
notes.explanation: Internal is also the default span kind if none is set when the span is created.

notes.front: A service inserts a job into a queue for another service to process later, asynchronously. What span kind does OpenTelemetry give the span that creates that job?
notes.back: Producer. Producer spans represent the creation of a job that may be processed asynchronously later.
notes.explanation: The child of a producer span is always a consumer span, even though the two may run far apart in time.

notes.front: A worker picks a queued job off a queue and processes it, long after the job was created. What span kind does OpenTelemetry give that span?
notes.back: Consumer. Consumer spans represent the processing of a job created by a producer.
notes.explanation: Its parent is always a producer span, even though the consumer span may start long after the producer span has ended.

notes.front: What’s the difference between a metric, a log and a trace?
notes.back: Metrics are numeric data aggregated over time. Logs are timestamped messages, not necessarily tied to a request. Traces record one request’s path, built from spans.
notes.explanation: Each answers a different question: metrics show that something changed, logs show a specific event happened, and traces show where a request went.
notes.contrast: Metrics aggregate numbers over time; logs are discrete timestamped messages; traces connect spans into one request’s journey.

notes.front: What are two advantages that Prometheus’s FAQ gives for pulling metrics rather than pushing them?
notes.back: You can start extra monitoring instances as needed (for example on your laptop) and more easily tell if a target is down.
notes.explanation: A third advantage the FAQ gives is that you can visit a target directly in a browser to inspect its health.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: An engineer wants to check a target’s health by opening it directly in a web browser, without running any extra tooling. Does this fit better with Prometheus’s pull model or a push model?
notes.back: The pull model — the FAQ notes you can manually visit a target and inspect its health with a web browser.
notes.explanation: With pulling, each target serves its own metrics over HTTP, so a person can open that same endpoint in a browser, just as Prometheus does when it scrapes.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: For cases where you must push metrics instead of being scraped, Prometheus offers an intermediary called the {{c1::Pushgateway}}.
notes.explanation: It exists precisely because pulling isn’t always possible, not because pushing is Prometheus’s preferred way of working.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: A short-lived batch job finishes and exits before Prometheus’s next scheduled scrape could ever reach it. Can Prometheus pull its metrics after it has already exited?
notes.back: No: once it has exited there is nothing to scrape. For a service-level batch job, this is what the Pushgateway is for.
notes.explanation: The job has to hand over its result before it exits. For a batch job tied to one machine, the docs recommend the Node Exporter’s textfile collector instead of the Pushgateway.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway

notes.front: What is the key difference between Prometheus’s pull model and a push model for collecting metrics?
notes.back: In the pull model, Prometheus fetches metrics from targets over HTTP. In a push model, targets send metrics to the collector themselves.
notes.explanation: The FAQ judges pulling only slightly better than pushing overall, and says it should not be a major point when choosing a monitoring system.
notes.contrast: Pull: the server decides when to fetch, and a missing target is obvious. Push: the target decides when to send, and a dead target is harder to spot.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Why do you pull rather than push?”

notes.front: According to Prometheus’s own guidance, what is usually the only valid use case for the Pushgateway?
notes.back: Capturing the outcome of a service-level batch job — one not tied to a specific machine or job instance.
notes.explanation: A service-level job’s metrics carry no machine or instance label, so they don’t go stale when a machine is renamed or removed. That matters because the Pushgateway never forgets pushed series unless they are deleted by hand.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, “Should I be using the Pushgateway?”

notes.front: A nightly cron job tied to one particular server runs a security update and exits. Prometheus’s docs recommend exposing its metrics through the Node Exporter’s textfile collector, not the Pushgateway. Why?
notes.back: Because the job is tied to a specific machine, and the Pushgateway is meant for service-level batch jobs, not machine-specific ones.
notes.explanation: Using the Pushgateway for a machine-tied job risks leaving its metrics behind forever if that machine is renamed or removed.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, “Alternative strategies”

notes.front: Besides static_configs, what are two service discovery mechanisms that Prometheus’s configuration reference lists for finding scrape targets?
notes.back: Any two of many: for example, file-based service discovery and Kubernetes service discovery. The reference also lists DNS, Consul and several cloud providers.
notes.explanation: Targets may be statically configured or dynamically discovered using one of several supported service-discovery mechanisms.

notes.front: A team’s targets change constantly as autoscaling adds and removes instances, and they’d rather not edit a config file by hand each time. Is a static_config or a service discovery mechanism the better fit?
notes.back: A service discovery mechanism. static_configs specify a fixed list of targets, which won’t track autoscaling on its own.
notes.explanation: Service discovery mechanisms such as the Kubernetes or file-based ones are built to stay synchronised with a changing set of targets.

notes.front: A static_config allows specifying a list of {{c1::targets}} and a common label set for them.
notes.explanation: It’s the canonical way to name static targets by hand in a scrape configuration.

notes.front: A team runs exactly two Prometheus exporters on two fixed hostnames that never change. Is a static_config a reasonable way to scrape them?
notes.back: Yes. static_configs is the canonical way to specify a fixed list of targets, which fits a small, unchanging set well.
notes.explanation: It only becomes awkward once the target list starts changing often, which is when a service discovery mechanism pays off instead.

notes.front: Kubernetes service discovery configurations always stay synchronised with the cluster state by retrieving scrape targets from Kubernetes’ {{c1::REST API}}.
notes.explanation: That live connection to the API is what lets Prometheus pick up new Pods and Services without a config reload.

notes.front: A cluster autoscaler adds and removes nodes and Pods throughout the day, and the team wants Prometheus’s target list to track this without manual edits. Which fits best: Kubernetes service discovery, or a static_config?
notes.back: Kubernetes service discovery. It stays synchronised with the cluster’s state automatically, which a fixed static_config cannot do.
notes.explanation: It reads live from the cluster’s REST API, so scaling events are picked up without touching the configuration file.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes service discovery role discovers one target per cluster node, defaulting to the kubelet’s HTTP port?
notes.back: The node role.
notes.explanation: Its target address defaults to the first available node address, in the order NodeInternalIP, NodeExternalIP, NodeLegacyHostIP, then NodeHostName.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes service discovery role discovers a target for each service port of each Service, useful for blackbox monitoring?
notes.back: The service role.
notes.explanation: It sets the target address to the Service’s Kubernetes DNS name and the matching port, rather than to any specific Pod.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes service discovery role discovers all Pods and exposes each container’s declared ports as a separate target?
notes.back: The pod role.
notes.explanation: If a container declares no ports, the pod role still creates a target for it without a port, so a port can be added by hand through relabeling.

notes.front: The endpoints role discovers targets from a Service’s listed endpoints, one per port. What does Prometheus’s documentation say about this role from Kubernetes v1.33 onward?
notes.back: That the underlying Endpoints API is deprecated, and it recommends switching to the endpointslice role instead.
notes.explanation: Prometheus still supports the endpoints role, but its own docs already steer configurations toward the newer API.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes service discovery role does Prometheus’s documentation now recommend in place of the deprecated endpoints role?
notes.back: The endpointslice role.
notes.explanation: It discovers one target per endpoint address referenced in an EndpointSlice object, and needs the discovery.k8s.io/v1 API.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes service discovery role discovers a target for each path of each Ingress, useful for blackbox monitoring of an Ingress?
notes.back: The ingress role.
notes.explanation: Its target address is set to the host specified in the Ingress spec, rather than to any Pod or Service behind it.

notes.front: A good SLI measures your service from the perspective of your {{c1::users}}.
notes.explanation: The primer’s example of an SLI is the speed at which a web page loads: something users experience directly.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: A team picks “the speed at which a web page loads” as one of its measurements. Is this an SLI, an SLO, or an SLA?
notes.back: An SLI — it’s a measurement of the service’s behaviour, not yet a target or a contract.
notes.explanation: It only becomes an SLO once a target value is attached to it, such as “under 200ms for 95% of loads”.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: An SLO is accomplished by attaching one or more SLIs to {{c1::business value}}.
notes.explanation: That’s what separates a bare measurement from an objective: the SLO connects the number to something the organisation cares about.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: A team commits to “checkout pages load in under 2 seconds for 99% of visits”, with no refund or penalty if they miss it. Is this best described as an SLO or an SLA?
notes.back: An SLO: a target for a measured service level, with none of the contractual consequences an SLA would add.
notes.explanation: The SRE book’s own test is to ask what happens if it’s missed: no explicit consequence points to an SLO, not an SLA.
notes.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4, “Service Level Objectives”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What turns an SLO into an SLA, according to the SRE book?
notes.back: Explicit consequences for meeting or missing the SLOs. Financial ones, such as a rebate or a penalty, are the easiest to spot.
notes.explanation: The book notes that people often say “SLA” when they mean an SLO; a so-called SLA violation is usually just a missed objective.
notes.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4, “Service Level Objectives”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A courier firm promises next-day delivery, and its contract with a retailer gives the retailer a refund for every late parcel. Is the refund clause part of an SLI, an SLO, or an SLA?
notes.back: An SLA. The refund is exactly the kind of explicit consequence that turns a delivery-time objective into an agreement.
notes.explanation: The delivery-time promise itself is the SLO; the refund clause is what makes the whole arrangement an SLA.
notes.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4, “Service Level Objectives”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can you tell an SLO from an SLA, using the SRE book’s own test?
notes.back: Ask what happens if the objectives are missed. No explicit consequence: almost certainly an SLO. An explicit penalty points to an SLA.
notes.explanation: Most people say “SLA” when they mean an SLO. A real SLA breach is a contract matter that could end up in court.
notes.contrast: SLO: a target value for a measured service level, with no attached consequence. SLA: the same kind of target, wrapped in a contract with explicit consequences for missing it.
notes.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4, “Service Level Objectives”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In OpenTelemetry’s observability primer, what question does reliability answer?
notes.back: “Is the service doing what users expect it to be doing?”
notes.explanation: So a system can be up 100% of the time and still be unreliable, if what it does while it is up isn’t what users expect.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”

notes.front: A shopping site is up 100% of the time, but clicking “Add to Cart” on a pair of black shoes sometimes adds the wrong item. Does 100% uptime alone make this a reliable service?
notes.back: No. Reliability asks whether the service does what users expect, and here it sometimes doesn’t, despite being up.
notes.explanation: This is the primer’s own example for reliability: being up is not the same as doing what users expect.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer, “Reliability and metrics”
